claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a metastable single-phase solid solution.
Mg and the other alloying elements are initially distributed homogeneously.
High-temperature exposure drives Mg segregation toward grain boundaries and interfacial regions.
Mg segregation accelerates nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic phases preferentially form along grain boundaries or interphase interfaces.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallics locally depletes the surrounding matrix of elements that contribute to a protective oxide film.
Elevated temperature enhances Mg diffusion and thereby promotes its local accumulation and precipitation.
Elemental depletion and segregation cause inhomogeneous oxide formation or an insufficiently protective oxide scale.
Compromise of oxide-scale continuity and integrity reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Compromise of the protective oxide scale reduces corrosion resistance.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate under oxidizing or corrosive exposure at approximately 600–900 °C.
Thermally aged samples will contain localized Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates relative to the initial state.
Thermally aged samples will develop discontinuous or compromised protective oxide layers relative to the initial state.
Thermally aged samples will show measurably poorer corrosion and oxidation resistance than the unaged control.
The as-cast or as-processed metastable alloy has a continuous, thin protective oxide scale.
At lower temperatures or shorter exposure durations, the alloy may retain its initial protective properties because segregation and precipitation remain kinetically limited.
The Mg diffusion rates and Mg-rich intermetallic-formation kinetics are not fully quantified.
